[h1]About the Game[/h1]
Orwell is a game in which you have to read through articles, conversations and the likes to find bits of information to uncover a terrorist act. Depending on which information you present or withold, your superiors gain a different image of a person - which in turn can affect the outcome of the story.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
If you expect action-packed run'n'gun gameplay, this game is not for you. Instead, try to see it more as a mystery/interactive puzzle game. You read through a person's Blog and try to understand their motivation. Suddenly, you realize that two people you were investigating had a connection to each other, and thus you delve deeper into the story.

[h1]Theme / Story[/h1]
It couldn't be more relevant or timely. The game touches subjects like terrorism, state surveillance, how much information we present of ourselves or how much power the state should have. I enjoyed the perspective of "The Man" very much, as usually these dystopian futures are experienced through resistance fighters (because guns!).

[h1]Would I recommend it?[/h1]
Yes and no. First of all, if you are one of those "This isn't a game"-people, you just won't have fun with it.
Second, if you are anxious to make the "wrong" choice in a game (like me, for instance - [i]Datachunk marked[/i]), then this game might be troublesome for you.

You see, I tend to play these games like this: First, I select which outcome I want to achieve (e.g. save person X) and then act how I believe this outcome can be achieved.
However, Orwell is far better experienced (in my opinion) to just "do" and let the events unfold.

But as I said, if you are anxious about making the wrong call, you might not enjoy this game.
If you are neither scared by that nor by "this-isn't-a-game"-sayers, then you might really enjoy this game. I picked it up at a sale and enjoyed my time with it - hopefully you will too.

This game is essentially a "choose your own adventure" detective novel wherein your decisions are all made by choosing which information to share with - or conceal from - the authorities. The concept is an interesting one and the game does throw up some nice surprises in both the gameplay and the plot, and there are occasional moments of humour.

However, the limitations in using conflicting information are rather annoying. For example sometimes the game will let you choose only one of two (or more) different pieces of information even when both are true and could be vital to successfully completing your objectives. (I get that this is a key game mechanic, but I think it could be explained or handled better to make the game feel less forced.) In particular there is one key decision which just comes down to a 50/50 guess with no supporting information to help the player make the correct choice. (I am talking about the part where the player must determine the third location - If I missed any clues as to which is the correct answer, somebody please tell me!)

Another major concern is the quality of the writing; whilst for the most part the writing is capable and there are some memorable moments, the writing is never compelling - I gave up reading about halfway through my first playthrough, instead just scanning text for the (conveniently highlighted) choices. Whilst I can forgive bad writing in some games, for a game that is all about the writing the standard really needs to be higher. Some of the text simply drags on too long, especially any form of dialogue (phone calls, chat text, etc.) - this is doubly annoying for dialogue as there is no way to skip it. (Usually you can just let it run in the background whilst you read other in-game documents, but be careful with this as some actions are time-critical.)

Replay value may depend how willing you are to work through the text again. Whilst it is nice to see the different outcomes your actions can have, it feels like 90% or more of the game remains identical so it becomes a slog to see the few changes or pick up achievements. Some of the achievements are so ambiguously described that the only way to complete them seems to be relying on lots of replays and blind luck, or of course walkthroughs.

It is a shame to see such a nice idea and plot wasted without sufficient polish, but if the devs learn from this I do look forward to seeing what else they can produce.

[h1] A very enjoyable game with hidden depth, despite the very simple game mechanics. [/h1]

You investigate persons of interest in a bombing (i.e read a whole bunch and invade peoples' privacy) through their online information and electronic devices via Orwell, The Nations new secret surveilence system. The people and ways you can investigate are not all immediately available, you unlock more options and imformation based on the data you upload and where you are in the story. The gameplay ultimately boils down to drag-and-droping the datachunks (that the game hightlights) that you think are relevent, into Orwell.

While on the surface the game may seem not very challenging or lacking in replayability as some claim, there are subtleties that make Orwell really great.

Such as the fact that you, as the investigator, are the only person who will see the [b] context [/b] of the data you're uploading. Mild episode 1 spoiler: [spoiler] See a woman joking with her boyfriend that she stole his credit card (which she uses to buy a bottle of wine), which he seems mildly annoyed by but seemingly fine with? Upload that into Orwell and all your superiors know is that she "stole a credit card". [/spoiler] Whether or not you think reporting that is morally right or not, it does have an effect on how things turn out for her.
There are several times such as this when the information you can upload is damning, incomplete or inaccurate simply because the datachunk lacks context. There are times when you can use this to your advantage, if say you want to frame someone winkwink.

There are also times where you will encounter "conflicting data chunks", where you have the choice of which one (sometimes if any) you wish to upload. These choices often lead to a person or circumstance being viewed in an entirely different manner. Sometimes it is the drastic difference between someone being seen as a terrorist or an innocent.
This is why it's very important to look very carefully at what a datachunk is really uploading to Orwell and remember you needn't and perhaps shouldn't upload everything.

Overall this game puts you into a position where you have to make a lot of moral decisions around privacy, relevancy, and generally be the judge of everyone you investigate. Your choices/ethics directly and indirectly influence the fate of all the characters you meet.

A brief note on replayability: I found there to be plenty of reasons to replay the game; be it for achievement hunting, because you messed up a lot the first time around (like me ^-^'), or just to see how everything pans out if you'd played differently. As of writing I have 11.3 hours on record and I still intend to play it further as I don't feel remotely done yet.
How much time you'll get out of it depends a lot on your playstyle and whether you're a completionist or someone who blitzes through games and doesn't bother with a replay.
The average time to finish your first run through seems to be around 4 or 5 hours for most people.

tldr: Tbh as long as you like detective and/or story-driven games, I whole-heartedly recommend Orwell. While I got it on sale, since playing I would totally pay full price.

P.S Try the demo because if you get to the end of it and feel the overwelming need to keep playing, you'll enjoy the full game.

PROS: I highly recommend everyone to play the DEMO of this game first. It'll give you a great feel of how the entire game is going to go, so you will know if you will like it or not. It's also a complete mind-screw as well, which was awesome. The soundtrack was very nice to listen to as well, and it's a smooth transitioning game with a great save-as-you-go feature.  It also has great replay value, so that you can get various outcomes.

CONS: I bought the game and flew through threw the chapters quickly. It's 5 Chapters and it takes about 4 hours to complete all chapters, if you take your time. 4 hours for a 10 dollar game is a bit steep for me. I usually like to get $1 for every hour of playtime, so the game pretty much pays for itself. Although there is replay value to this game, I still don't like how quickly it goes by. The game was also a bit slow and laggy in some spots, like moving datachunks while text was still steaming. 

Overall it's a great quick game, but I would recommend searching for it on sale, and I would also recommend DEMOing the game first. It's definitely not a game made for everyone, but it's got a lot of good going for it!

I can't imagine the replayability will be very high, but -- the premise of this game is both great and also very important. Working as a covert tech obtaining info publicly available online in order to put together information on suspects/targets can help shed light on just how much personal information is readily available on almost all people this day and age-- even this review. With due diligence, one can find tons of info on just about anyone. It freaks a lot of people out and seeing a Blue's Clue's version (closest analogy I could think of, game is not much like Blues Clues) might help ameliorate that. A popular tactic of authorities of any sort (hiring managers, law enforcement, parents, whatever) is to comb through someone's social media profile. -- and yet apparently people are still taken aback when someone finds and looks through their facebook profile. 

Anyway... this game addresses a lot of currently important social issues in an engaging and thought-provoking way. It's unique and fun and somehow manages this with being almost entirely text-based.

I cannot begin to describe how pleasantly surprised I was by this game. There are just so many things to love about it. To begin with, the story is incredibly immersive and has a very genuine feel to it. The characters are believable and makes readers/players identify and feel attachment to them. While the mechanics are incredibly simple, they are appropriate to the game itself, and make you feel as though you are part of one big social experiment to see what you would do.

I do not wish to spoil the ending, but I love the twist and decisions you face at the end. There is truly no win-win situation for everyone and I love it! It makes your choice as the player that much harder.

I can see a huge use for this game in the future. This would be a fantastic game for the classroom. Whether you have an English class learning about Orwell's "1984" and needing a modern example to explain it, or in a Social Studies class to explore the implications of invading privacy to take down terrorists, I could see this being a very versitile game. True, the strong language used might be an issue and prevent it from being a "perfect" choice for schools, but I see the potential.

If there is one thing I would like to see changed/added, it's the replayability. You can bang out all the endings and choices in the course of a couple of days, leaving very little else to do. Some randomized missions or even a second season of episodes would really make this pop as a game. However, that may just have to be something I hope for out of a sequel. Overall, this was a great play and I would indeed recommend it to others. My only hope is that we'll see more of the Orwell game in the future.

So I just finished my second playthrough and I'm highly inclined to replay it again in order to get another ending. I find Orwell to be a fantasticly entertaining game that tested my attention and combination skills. I really liked the case and the parts of the story that turned out slightly different whenever I did or didn't upload certain data chunks. The endings were frustratingly unsatisfying but because of that all the more realistic and refreshing - so far there was no possible way to have an entirely 'good' ending because no matter what there was always something not sitting well with my conscience. I applaud the developers for daring to leave some kind of open ending to the game.

The only thing I found annoying was that whenever I didn't pay enough attention to what data I was uploading and uploaded information that was false or misleading, I couldn't revert the change and I had to replay the entire chapter to get to the same point again. Which sometimes led to me making the same mistake AGAIN because I clicked through all of it too fast without paying attention, so I had to repeat the same thing again. I know the game tells you to stay on your guard in order to avoid uploading bullshit data, but a simple 'delete data' or 'change data' button would have made this a lot easier.

Oh yeah, the topic of government surveillance as portrayed throughout the game was both intriguing and scaring. It makes you wonder how far governments in real life intend to go in order to guarantee for their respective nations' security. No matter what your opinion on this matter is, there's no saying in what the 'correct' procedure is - spying on every citizen and evaluating on that base is no solution, but neither is leaving people to their own devices and letting potential threats go unchecked.

To everyone interested in this topic, I would highly recommend this fantastic game.

Having followed this game for a while, waiting for the episodes to release, and meeting the devs at PAX, I can say that this was probably one of the most unique "point and click" experiences I've ever had. I can't even go into much detail, because I truly want you to experience this game for yourself, but there are a few things I will say:

+The game really does a good job of making the in-game world feel "real". From a terse, yet thorough, well-thought explanation to "The Nation's" geopolitcal standing, to the online advertisements and clickbait filler that often pepper the relevant articles

+All of the characters have very distinct, memorable lives, and you'll have a chance to explore each and every one of them. There are no characters which get passed over, and this really drives home the point that what you're doing is very 1984. You're not just seeing information relevant to your case, you're seeing ALL of the information.

+The audio. There is, quite frankly, very little music or ambient noise in the game, but this is actually a positive point for this title. Whenever you come across a particularly shocking datachunk, this intense riff plays, and maintains itself until you move on. I often found myself hearing the music before I realized what I was actually looking at, and it made me super excited to keep reading.

-The episodes did feel rather short, despite there being a lot of content in each. This is offset by the fact that you're not paying per episode. When you buy the game, you get the whole game, not just episode one.

-There was a mechanic near the end (not a spoiler), where you are given a limit on how many data chunks you could upload, given the explanation that "as you know, datachunks cost time". This was never really well illustrated in earlier episodes, and, while you were scolded for uploading silly or irrelevant information (such as Cassandra's location being "over the rainbow and into wonderland" in the first episode), you were never really penalized at all unless you uploaded the incorrect answer for a conflicting (yellow) datachunk. I think the entire "limited datachunk" mechanic could have been implemented a bit better, since the player was previously unprepared to deal with that. I think that perhaps an actual time limit (via countdown timer) would have made the whole thing seem a bit more frenzied, instead of the player idly dawdling, and having time to carefully consider their decisions.


All in all, this was a great game, and I seriously look forward to seeing more great ideas come out of this developer!

Okay... I don't usually write game reviews. I generally have a pretty good idea of what I'm buying beforehand on Steam, and if a game is shit it's usually because I paid for shit. But this fucking game got me.

The biggest trick is that little "Choice Matters" tag that people gave it. I love choice games. The replay value of finding every unique ending alone usually makes it worth the price. There's also something thrilling, something special to video games, when you're able to make a choice and know it matters.

Choice doesn't matter in this game.

You do ultimately get to choose what's "shown" to your supervisor, and sometimes those choices do affect the game in some way. But you're railroaded HARD through just about every major event, forced to fight for even the smallest change in dialogue from game to game. The only half-consequential "choice" you get comes at the end, and to get there you need to sit through 2+ hours of the exact same gameplay. You might as well be buying the game to play once. If you're ok with playing once and then quitting (the game does have some beautiful artwork and some really gripping moments) then by all means do so. But if you want your choices to really matter, don't buy Orwell.

Instead, the game presents one scenario that plays out over a five-day period. The game-mechanics themselves are not complicated and the games graphics and presentation is mostly text and still-pictures, so more scenarios should not be difficult or time-consuming to add later on.

"Big Brother has arrived - and it’s you." In Orwell, you are tasked to report to the government on potential threats. You use the all powerful Orwell spying software to gleam every bit of info from any deemed suspicious. The catch is that you work with a supervisor who can speak to you, but you cannot speak to them. The only thing the supervisor sees from you are the snippets of information you send them, so you have to be careful that what you send will not be taken out of context.

Orwell is an interactive story, where your choices matter. The entire story is told through text and images, there is no voice acting. If you like text adventure games/interactive fiction or choose-your-own-adventure books, you will like this game, you'll also enjoy it if you want to feel like a detective piecing together clues. If you don't like reading, this is not the game for you. It's hard to compare this game to another because the gameplay is rather unique. I came into this game from Stories Untold and Event[0] looking for more games that tell a story and require you to think, and I was not disappointed.

I recently read George Orwell's [i] 1984, [/i] which really made me think about what in society is right or wrong. In Orwell's [i] 1984, [/i] we follow Winston Smith, an ordinary member of the Outer Party, who is fighting against the Party's ideas in his own way. [spoiler] However, we find out that the Party has been watching him the whole time, as well as watching his partner Julia. [/spoiler] The game, [i] Orwell, [/i] does an amazing job of modernizing George Orwell's work, and instead of having the protagonist try their best in working against the Party, the protagonist is working on the side of the law. During my first playthrough, I thought working on the side of justice wasn't half bad. I was putting people behind bars for criminal acts. I had no thoughts thinking that what I was doing was wrong. Except, when human life was put at risk [spoiler] (for example; Nina Maternova), [/spoiler] I started thinking that perhaps, I wasn't doing the right thing. The longer I played, the more I detested the people I was working for, as their motives were different from mine. I wanted to bring peace to the world, not fear. All they wanted was to catch individuals they deemed "potentially dangerous." All in all, I'd recommend this game to anyone who has enjoyed George Orwell's work, and also to people who like playing games that have underlying meanings.

'Orwell' is a fascinating first-person adventure game that explores the implications of online surveillance -- by having the player act as Big Brother! You play an investigator tasked with capturing perpetrators responsible for a lethal bombing. With the help of an investigative advisor, you collect Datachunks to build profiles of suspects.

However, profile building is not a rote task because you'll need to pore through online documents, phone and chat transcripts, resolve conflicting information, and be judicious and definitive about which Datachunk to add to the profiles. Given that, your decisions in building a suspect's profile will have both short-term and long-term consequences, affecting how the story unfolds. 

'Orwell' makes players reflect on, or perhaps even reconsider the value of and impact of surveillance on public safety. It's both entertaining and thought-provoking, and I was compelled to replay it twice more so that I can see how different decisions will yield different outcomes. With such high value in entertainment, intellectual stimulation and replayability for its price, 'Orwell' gets my enthusiastic recommendation.
If you ever wanted to find out what it's like working for the NSA but you want to keep your dignity, this game is for you.
